## The ticket

Your new Quality Analyst's first week ends with her handing you two things: an org chart
and the table of contents from Lakeshore's quality manual. You expected the org chart to
make sense immediately — it does, mostly. The table of contents doesn't. It's organized
into ten sections with headers like "Process Control," "Assessments: Internal and
External," and "Deviations, Nonconformances, and Adverse Events." Nowhere does it say
"change management." Nowhere does it say "incident." Nowhere does it say "knowledge base."

"This is how AABB structures it," she says, meaning the American Association of Blood
Banks, Lakeshore's accrediting body. "Everything we do lives in one of these ten
buckets. It's called the QSE framework — Quality System Essentials."

Three weeks later, an AABB assessor is on-site for Lakeshore's accreditation survey. In
the closing meeting she says, almost in passing, "I didn't see your change-control
process cross-referenced anywhere under Process Control." Your Quality Analyst nods like
this is a completely normal sentence. You don't, yet — but you're the one who has to sit
in that room and sound like you belong there, and you can't do that by re-reading the
org chart. You need the buckets themselves, and you need to know how they map onto
things you already run.

## Why this framework exists — and the ITIL bridge

Start with what a "quality system" actually is, because the term gets used loosely.
It's not the Quality department, and it isn't quality control (the testing that checks
whether a specific unit or process met spec). A quality system is the whole
organizational machine — policies, processes, procedures, records, people, and
oversight — built to make sure the organization reliably does what it says it does, and
can prove it. Quality control is one input into that machine, not the machine itself.

AABB didn't invent this idea; it packaged it. In 1997, AABB launched a defined set of
Quality System Essentials — the original QSEs — as a deliberate shift in the industry's
posture: from *catching* errors after the fact (inspect the output, reject the bad
units) to *preventing* them by controlling the process that produces the output in the
first place. That shift followed a period in which FDA had been citing blood
establishments for basic good-manufacturing-practice gaps — a track record that made
"we caught it before it shipped" look a lot less reassuring than it used to. AABB
updated the QSE template again in 2023, and current AABB Standards editions are built on
that updated structure. The number of QSEs has stayed at **ten** across that update; some
chapter titles have shifted slightly in wording edition to edition, but the ten themes
haven't.

Here's the bridge, and it's a genuinely close one, not a stretch: **a QSE framework is
functionally the same move as ITIL's service value chain and practices.** You already
run a set of interlocking practices — incident, problem, change enablement,
configuration management, service catalog, continual improvement — specifically so that
your organization's operational work is structured, auditable, and comparable across
teams and time, instead of ad hoc and tribal-knowledge-dependent. That's exactly what
the QSEs are for, aimed at a quality system instead of a service management system. You
are not learning a new kind of thinking here. You're learning AABB's vocabulary for a
kind of thinking you already do daily.

The single strongest version of this bridge: **ISO 9001, the international quality
management standard, and ISO/IEC 20000-1, the IT service management standard, share the
same harmonized clause structure** — context, leadership, planning, support, operation,
performance evaluation, improvement (clauses 4 through 10, under ISO's common "Annex
SL"-style framework used across multiple management-system standards). If you've worked
near an ISO 20000 or ISO 27001 certification, you've seen this shape before, even if
nobody called it that. AABB's QSEs aren't literally ISO 9001's clauses — they're AABB's
own framework — but they organize the same underlying territory: who's accountable,
what resources and competence are required, how work is controlled, how you document and
keep records, how you catch and fix what goes wrong, how you check whether the whole
system is actually working. A blood center's quality system and an IT service management
system are answering the same category of question about two different kinds of "product."

A few concrete pairings, at the level of "which drawer does this go in," not a full
crosswalk (that full mapping is its own future lesson, and it's worth more depth than a
single-lesson table can give it):

- **Documents and Records** ↔ knowledge management, and to a lesser extent
  configuration management for the controlled-copy problem.
- **Deviations, Nonconformances, and Adverse Events** ↔ incident management.
- **Process Improvement** ↔ problem management, specifically the root-cause and
  permanent-fix half of it.
- **Process Control**, which is where change control sits ↔ change enablement.
- **Supplier and Customer Issues** ↔ supplier management.
- **Assessments: Internal and External** ↔ your own internal audits and service
  reviews, feeding a continual-improvement register.

Hold those loosely for now. Every later module in this course opens by naming which QSE
it lives in, and by the time you've been through all of them, these pairings will be
concrete instead of abstract. This lesson's job is narrower: give you the map, not the
tour.

## The framework in plain English

**QSE (Quality System Essential)** is AABB's term for one of ten defined categories that
together organize every requirement in its accreditation standards. Think of it as ten
labeled drawers. Every policy, procedure, record, and control a blood establishment
maintains gets filed into exactly one of them (sometimes more than one, when a topic
genuinely spans categories — more on that below). An AABB assessor doesn't audit
Lakeshore department by department; she audits QSE by QSE, checking that each drawer is
actually full of what its label promises, not just labeled.

A structural note before the list: this session verified the ten-QSE structure directly
from AABB's own public material — including a dated, effective document (a proposed
edition of AABB's Standards with a real effective date that has already passed) — but
AABB doesn't post a single plain "here is the current definitive list" page, and the
exact wording of a chapter title has drifted slightly between editions. Treat the names
below as accurate to the theme, and double-check exact current wording against whatever
edition is on Lakeshore's shelf before you put a title in a document that has to survive
word-for-word scrutiny.

The ten QSEs, in AABB's own numbering:

1. **Organization** — who's accountable. Executive management's responsibility and
   authority for the quality system, management review of its effectiveness, and who has
   authority to approve an exception to policy.
2. **Resources** — staffing, qualifications, and competence. Job descriptions, training,
   competence assessment, continuing education.
3. **Equipment** — equipment (including IT systems, explicitly) selection,
   qualification, use, monitoring, and maintenance.
4. **Supplier and Customer Issues** — qualifying suppliers and managing customer
   agreements. (You'll see this titled slightly differently across documents —
   "Supplier and Customer Agreements" in one, "Suppliers and Customers" in another —
   same drawer, different label on it.)
5. **Process Control** — the largest of the ten in most editions: validating processes,
   and controlling how the actual operational work — including change control — gets
   done correctly and consistently.
6. **Documents and Records** — the document lifecycle (draft through retirement) and
   record retention.
7. **Deviations, Nonconformances, and Adverse Events** — capturing, assessing,
   investigating, and disposing of anything that fails to meet a requirement, plus
   reporting some of those events to outside agencies (FDA, in Lakeshore's case).
8. **Assessments: Internal and External** — Lakeshore's own internal quality
   assessments, plus supporting external assessments by AABB, FDA, and other regulators.
9. **Process Improvement** — corrective and preventive action: fixing not just the
   instance, but the process that allowed it.
10. **Facilities and Safety** — physical space, environmental monitoring, and
    occupational and biohazard safety.

Two things worth flagging explicitly. First: a real activity can touch more than one
QSE. A document revision that changes a validated process is a Documents and Records
event *and* a Process Control event, and a good quality system's cross-references say so
rather than pretending it fits neatly in one drawer. Second: this course spends its next
six modules living almost entirely inside QSEs 5, 6, 7, and 9 — process control (change),
documents and records, deviations, and process improvement (CAPA) — because that's where
an IT Director's regulated work concentrates. QSEs 1 through 4, 8, and 10 matter and
you'll place things in them, but they're not where you'll spend depth in this course.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| 21 CFR 606.100(d) | "Six-oh-six point one-hundred, paragraph d" | Permits a facility to build its SOPs on named organizations' manuals — AABB's by name — as long as those procedures are at least as strict as Part 606 itself. | The one place FDA's own regulatory text names AABB directly. It doesn't adopt the QSE framework as federal law; it lets Lakeshore use AABB's structure as a floor to build on. |

One callback worth having open next to this table: the `regulatory-landscape-orientation`
foundation already built a full citation-format decoder for statute, FDA regulation, FDA
guidance, and AABB Standard — including the rule that an AABB Standard is cited by
number and title only, never quoted verbatim, because the text is copyrighted. Everything
in this lesson about the QSEs follows that same rule: names and themes, never AABB's
actual requirement text.

## The actual text

Quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/606.100.md`, retrieved from eCFR — this is the same
606.100 that two earlier foundation lessons already grounded, now read for what it says
about AABB specifically:

> (d) In addition to the requirements of this subpart and in conformity with this
> section, any facility may utilize current standard operating procedures such as the
> manuals of the organizations, as long as such specific procedures are consistent with,
> and at least as stringent as, the requirements contained in this part.
>
> (1) American Association of Blood Banks.

Read that carefully, the same way you'd read a vendor contract clause a lawyer flagged.
It's permission, not adoption. It says Lakeshore *may* build its SOPs on AABB's manuals
as a starting point — provided the result is at least as strict as Part 606's own
requirements. It does not say the QSE framework itself is an FDA requirement, and it
does not hand AABB's Standards FDA's enforcement authority. An earlier module in this
curriculum confirmed, by searching Part 606's full text, that "AABB" appears exactly
once in the entire part's regulatory text — right here, in 606.100(d). Every other place
AABB shows up in Lakeshore's world is accreditation-tier, not regulation-tier. That single
fact is the cleanest possible proof that the QSE framework and Part 606 are two separate
obligations that happen to overlap in subject matter, not one obligation wearing two
names.

## What an inspector or assessor would actually look for

An FDA investigator doesn't ask about QSEs. That vocabulary is AABB's, not FDA's, and an
investigator's checklist runs off Part 606 and related CFR sections directly — a point
worth holding onto, because it's easy to let QSE language creep into a document you'll
later hand to FDA, where it will read as an unfamiliar and slightly confusing dialect.

An **AABB assessor** is a different conversation entirely, and this is where the QSE
structure becomes the actual audit trail. She isn't checking whether Lakeshore's quality
manual *uses* the right ten headers — that's necessary, not sufficient. She's checking
whether each QSE has real, working substance behind its label: does "Process Control"
actually contain a change-control process with records showing it's followed, not just a
section header with that name and nothing filed under it? Does "Assessments: Internal
and External" show evidence of internal audits actually happening on schedule, with
findings that go somewhere, not a policy stating that they should? The artifact she
wants is a **cross-reference or index** — something that maps Lakeshore's actual SOPs,
records, and org-chart accountabilities onto each of the ten QSEs — maintained by
whoever owns the quality manual, typically your Quality Analyst or the quality
department more broadly. A quality manual with the right ten section headers and thin or
missing content underneath one of them is exactly the gap the assessor in this lesson's
opening scenario just caught: "I didn't see your change-control process cross-referenced
anywhere under Process Control" is another way of saying "the label exists; I couldn't
find the drawer's contents."

## Common traps

**"The QSEs are an FDA requirement."** They're not, and this is worth stating plainly
because it's the easiest possible mislabeling in this whole lesson. Using the
`regulatory-landscape-orientation` foundation's four-tier framework: the QSE structure
sits at the AABB Standard tier — binding on Lakeshore because Lakeshore holds AABB
accreditation, enforced through accreditation assessment, not federal inspection. 606.100(d)
is the one clause where FDA's own text touches AABB by name, and even there it's
permission to use AABB's manuals as an SOP floor, not an adoption of AABB's framework as
federal law. Calling a QSE gap "an FDA violation" in an internal report or a CAB
conversation overstates the consequence and points people at the wrong regulator when
they go looking for the fix.

**"Our quality manual just needs the right section headers."** This is the failure mode
the assessor's comment in the opening scenario catches directly. Structure without
substance — ten correctly labeled sections with real content under some of them and
thin or copied-language filler under others — reads to an assessor exactly like a change
ticket with a filled-in template and no actual impact assessment behind it: the form is
right, the work isn't there. The QSE headers are a map for organizing genuine quality
work, not a compliance checkbox you satisfy by having the right table of contents.

## What this means for your job

- **Learn the ten QSE names well enough to place any quality activity in one (or name
  which two it spans) without looking it up.** That's the whole finish line of this
  lesson, and it's the vocabulary every later module and every AABB assessor
  conversation assumes you already have.
- **When your Quality Analyst cites a QSE by name, ask what's actually filed under it,
  not whether the label is correct.** "We have a Process Control section" tells you
  nothing an assessor would accept. "Here's the change-control SOP and the last six
  months of change records cross-referenced under Process Control" does.
- **Don't let "QSE" and "FDA requirement" blur together in a document that leaves your
  building.** A deviation report, a CAB packet, or an inspection response that cites a
  QSE gap as if it were a Part 606 violation is a mislabeling error an inspector or
  assessor will both notice — for opposite reasons.
- **Use the ISO 9001 / ITIL bridge to orient yourself fast in an unfamiliar quality
  conversation, then verify the specific mapping before you act on it.** "This sounds
  like change enablement" is a good first instinct and a bad final answer — QSE-land
  demands more than ITIL does in ways the next several modules will spell out one at a
  time.
- **Ask for the cross-reference index, not just the manual's table of contents.**
  If Lakeshore's quality system doesn't have a document mapping SOPs and records to each
  QSE, that's a gap worth raising before an assessor finds it first.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Your Quality Analyst says, "AABB Standards require us to organize our quality manual into these ten QSE sections — it's a federal requirement." Accurate?

Half right, in a way that matters. AABB Standards do require Lakeshore's quality system
to be built on the QSE structure — that part is accurate, and because Lakeshore is
AABB-accredited, it's practically mandatory. But "federal requirement" is wrong. This is
the AABB Standard tier from the `regulatory-landscape-orientation` foundation, not the
FDA regulation tier: binding on Lakeshore through accreditation, enforced by AABB
assessment, not by FDA inspection. The one place FDA's own text touches AABB is 606.100(d),
which permits using AABB's manuals as an SOP floor — it doesn't make the QSE framework
itself a federal requirement. Correcting "federal requirement" to "AABB accreditation
requirement" isn't pedantic; citing the wrong regulator in a written response is the kind
of error that undermines credibility with both of them.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: A change to a validated blood-processing procedure gets revised, approved, and reissued. Which QSE does that activity belong to?

Both Process Control and Documents and Records, genuinely — this is the "touches more
than one drawer" case flagged above, not a trick question with one right answer. The
change itself — assessing the change's impact, getting it approved, validating it if
needed — lives in Process Control. Once approved, revising the controlled document,
issuing the new version, and retiring the old one is a Documents and Records activity.
A quality manual that cross-references this kind of event under both QSEs is doing it
right; one that forces it into only one is hiding half the audit trail.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: The AABB assessor's comment in this lesson's opening scenario — "I didn't see your change-control process cross-referenced anywhere under Process Control" — what gap is she actually pointing at?

Not a missing section header (the QSE structure format assumption is already satisfied)
and not a Part 606 violation (QSEs aren't FDA's vocabulary). She's pointing at a
structure-without-substance gap: the Process Control drawer exists and is labeled
correctly, but the actual change-control process and its records aren't indexed under
it, so she can't find the evidence that it's real and working. The fix isn't rewording a
header — it's building or fixing the cross-reference that connects the label to the
actual SOPs and records behind it.
:::

## Where this goes next

You now have the map: ten QSEs, what each one covers, and how the whole framework sits
relative to Part 606 and to the ITIL practices you already run. The next module,
`deviations-and-nonconformances`, opens by naming its QSE — Deviations, Nonconformances,
and Adverse Events — and takes a real event at Lakeshore from discovery all the way
through containment, impact assessment, product disposition, and a documented
reportability decision. That's this framework's seventh drawer, opened up in full.
